content: Albuterol is a medication prescribed to prevent and treat wheezing, difficulty breathing, and chest tightness caused by lung diseases such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD refers to a group of diseases that affect the lungs and airways. Albuterol belongs to a class of medications known as bronchodilators. It works by relaxing and opening the air passages in the lungs, making it easier to breathe. Albuterol is available in several forms, including tablets, syrup, and extended-release (long-acting) tablets, all of which are taken orally. The regular tablets and syrup are typically taken three or four times a day, while the extended-release tablets are usually taken once every 12 hours. It is important to take albuterol at the same times each day. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take albuterol exactly as directed. Do not take more or less of it, or take it more frequently than prescribed by your doctor. Swallow the extended-release tablets whole with plenty of water or other liquids. Do not split, chew, or crush them. Your doctor may start you on a low dose of albuterol and gradually increase your dose. While albuterol can help control your symptoms, it does not cure your condition. Continue taking albuterol even if you feel well, and do not stop taking it without consulting your doctor. Contact your doctor if your symptoms worsen or if you feel that albuterol is no longer effective in controlling your symptoms. This medication may also be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking albuterol, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to albuterol, any other medications, or any of the ingredients in albuterol tablets, extended-release tablets, or capsules. Ask your pharmacist for a list of the ingredients. Additionally, inform your doctor and pharmacist about all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are currently taking or plan to take. Be sure to mention beta blockers (e.g., atenolol, labetalol, metoprolol, nadolol, propranolol), digoxin, diuretics (water pills), epinephrine, other oral or inhaled asthma medications, and medications for colds. Also, inform your doctor if you are taking or have recently stopped taking antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline, amoxapine, clomipramine, desipramine, doxepin, imipramine, nortriptyline, protriptyline, trimipramine) or monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors (e.g., isocarboxazid, phenelzine, selegiline, tranylcypromine). Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you closely for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have or have ever had an irregular heartbeat, heart disease, high blood pressure, hyperthyroidism (an overactive thyroid), diabetes, or seizures. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking albuterol, contact your doctor immediately. Be aware that albuterol can sometimes cause wheezing and difficulty breathing. If this occurs, stop using albuterol and contact your doctor right away. Do not use albuterol again unless your doctor advises you to do so. Unless instructed otherwise by your doctor, continue your normal diet while taking albuterol. If you miss a dose of albuterol, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Albuterol may cause side effects. Inform your doctor if any of the following symptoms are severe or persistent: nervousness, shakiness, dizziness, headache, uncontrollable shaking of a part of the body, muscle cramps, excessive motion or activity, sudden mood changes, nosebleeds, nausea, changes in appetite, difficulty falling or staying asleep, or pale skin. Some side effects can be serious. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of the following: fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat; chest pain; fever; blisters or rash; hives; itching; swelling of the face, throat, tongue, lips, eyes, hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs; increased difficulty breathing; difficulty swallowing; or hoarseness. Albuterol may cause other side effects. Contact your doctor if you experience any unusual problems while taking this medication. Store albuterol in the container it came in, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature and away from excess heat and moisture (do not store it in the bathroom). Dispose of any outdated or no longer needed medication. Consult your pharmacist about the proper disposal of your medication. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Symptoms of overdose may include seizures, chest pain, fast or irregular heartbeat, nervousness, headache, uncontrollable shaking of a part of the body, dry mouth, nausea, dizziness, excessive tiredness, lack of energy, and difficulty falling or staying asleep. Keep all appointments with your doctor. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have any questions about refilling your prescription.
